questions.q: What was the barter system, and what problems led to the invention of money?
answer: The barter system was the direct exchange of goods for other goods or services, without the use of money, and it worked in early, simple societies.

answer.text: Barter faced serious difficulties. It required a double coincidence of wants, meaning each person had to want exactly what the other offered. There was no common measure of value, so it was hard to say how much of one good equalled another. Many goods were indivisible, like a cow that could not be split for small purchases, and perishable goods could not easily store value.
To overcome these problems, money was invented as a common medium of exchange accepted by everyone, making buying, selling and saving far easier.

questions.q: Trace the evolution of money and explain its main functions.

answer.text: Money developed in stages. First came commodity money such as cattle, grain, salt and cowrie shells; then metal coins of gold, silver and copper; then paper currency notes; and finally modern forms like bank money, cards and digital UPI payments.

Money serves four main functions. It is a medium of exchange, accepted by all for buying and selling; a measure of value, giving a common yardstick to price goods; a store of value, since it can be saved for the future; and a standard of deferred payment, used to settle debts and instalments later.

answer: In India the currency is the Rupee, and currency notes are issued by the Reserve Bank of India.

questions.q: What different forms has money taken through history?
answer: Money has taken many forms over the ages, each an improvement on the one before.

answer.text: In early times, useful things themselves served as money. People used cattle, grain, salt, shells and similar goods as a common means of exchange, but these were hard to carry, store and divide.
Later, people began to use pieces of metal, and then stamped metal coins of gold, silver and copper. Coins were durable, easy to carry and of known value, so they were widely accepted.

As trade grew, paper currency, or notes, came into use, being lighter and easier to handle. Today money also takes the form of bank deposits and digital money, used through cheques, cards and mobile phones.

answer: Thus money evolved from goods to metal coins to paper notes and now to digital forms, becoming ever easier to use.

questions.q: What is the role of the Reserve Bank of India in the country's money?

answer.text: The Reserve Bank of India, or RBI, is the central bank of the country and controls the money and banking of India.

The RBI has the sole authority to print and issue currency notes, except the one-rupee note and coins, which are issued by the government. Every note carries the promise and signature of the RBI, which makes it acceptable as legal money everywhere in India.
The RBI also acts as banker to the government and to other banks, keeps the value of money steady, controls the supply of money and credit, and works to keep prices and the economy stable.

answer: Thus the RBI issues the country's currency and manages its money and banking to keep the economy stable.
